questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Unique opportunity: It’s not every day that you get the chance to go all the way to Australia. The opportunity to study in such a distant and unique country was a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I couldn’t miss. It was also important for me to go to an English-speaking country to further improve my English skills but also benefit my academic and professional pursuits.

Academic reputation: The host university is Australia’s biggest university and is renowned for its strong academic programs, particularly in my field of study. I was excited about the opportunity to enhance my academic knowledge and skills, especially by undertaking units that the University of Copenhagen do not offer. The university offered a wide range of units to choose from, providing me with the flexibility to tailor my studies according to my interests and career goals, which was a crucial aspect of my decision.

Cultural experience: Particularly, I wanted to learn about the unique cultural aspects of the destination. I believe that understanding diverse cultures is crucial for personal growth and global awareness, especially because we do not learn much about the importance of culture, which has a significant influence on public health.

Geographical location: The destination’s location was ideal for exploring other parts of Australia by being situated in a central location with good transportation links. The opportunity to travel around and explore the rest of Australia was highly appealing, and the country's diverse landscapes and unique wildlife were significant attractions for me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, my study abroad experience was very positive and unforgettable. While the academic level at the university was somewhat lower than I had expected, I believe this was partly due to the specific units I chose, some of which were at the undergraduate level. However, this allowed me to have more free time to travel, meet new people, and explore the country, which was a significant part of the exchange experience.

Socially, there were fewer organized events and the introduction to the university and fellow students was different from what I had anticipated, and it was easier to meet people outside of the university as many lectures were conducted online. This balance of academics and social life contributed to a highly rewarding overall experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy. You were well-guided both by your home university and the host university. I also feel that the most work was before the exchange, and once you were there, it was mostly about getting settled with the new university’s programs and finding your way with the units.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The orientation and introduction were different from what I expected, with fewer organized social events and a different approach to getting to know fellow students. The assistance was good, if needed. Overall, I was still very satisfied with my host institution.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy and went quickly once I was in Melbourne. I will especially recommend Flatmates Finders, which worked really well for me. If you’re looking to pay around 400 AUD per week (1600 AUD per month), which is a standard price for Melbourne CBD outside of student accommodations, it’s a great option.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Living off campus can be a bit different from student accommodations. I missed having more people around and the social events that come with it. On the plus side, having a place with fewer roommates (I had two) was nice because it gave me a retreat after meeting so many new people in other settings.

I did face some stress with my first roommates, as it didn’t work out to live with them, and I had to move and find new roommates while juggling assignments and studies. But luckily it was easy to find a new place to live. Living in Melbourne CBD was awesome—often with pool and gym access included when renting through Flatmates Finders. It can be more inconvenient to live off-campus, but it’s worth it in the end. It’s also a bit cheaper than student accommodation and saves you money on transport depending on where your campus is located.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was a bit disappointed that Monash University doesn’t offer housing near Caulfield Campus, especially since Clayton Campus was an hour away from the city. It would have been great to live around Caulfield or have some student accommodation options in the CBD, so I wouldn’t have had to find housing on my own. That said, there are pros and cons to everything, and in the end, I was happy living off-campus in the CBD - but I also don’t have anything else to compare it to.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was quite easy; I don’t recall having any major problems with it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: To be honest, I don’t really remember the details of the registration process, but I do recall that I was well-guided throughout and they had detailed guides and support available if any issues came up.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Detailed guides and personal assistance

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty successful. I corresponded with someone from Monash’s exchange office who helped me sign up for the units I wanted. There was a mention of a policy about how many undergraduate courses I could take, but they couldn’t provide details on it. I also pointed out that the main concern was whether my home university would accept the credits. After that, they updated my registration to include the units I wanted, which were approved by the University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to thoroughly review all the information sent by both your home and host universities - they provide detailed guides and are ready to help if you run into any issues.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I was very satisfied. The units were generally great, and I learned a lot of new things while getting introduced to the Australian system. However, it was a bit disappointing that many lectures were pre-recorded and reused from the Covid-19 period. While this made things more flexible at times, I missed better interaction with my classmates. There were also a few instances where the content wasn’t quite updated. On the whole, the lecturers were very engaged and passionate about their subjects, which was a big plus.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
As mentioned earlier, the level of the units was somewhat lower than what I was used to from the University of Copenhagen. However, I didn’t see this as a disadvantage. It meant less stress and allowed more time for other important aspects of the exchange experience. It was nice not to worry too much about passing.

There were two undergraduate courses that were a bit too easy, almost to the point of being demotivating. Despite this, I still learned a lot, even though the support was more hands-on. One of the courses was very easy for the instructors, which was a bit disappointing because a lot of the content was relevant, but the course design felt a bit lazy.

Additionally, the assignment requirements were quite strict, and often didn’t provide enough space or word count to include all the examples and details they asked for. This made the requirements somewhat superficial, as the format didn’t allow for a thorough exploration of the topics.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching at my host institution was quite different from UCPH. There was more online teaching, including lectures, which was a shift from what I was used to. On the plus side, all relevant materials were available online, and I didn’t have to spend money on textbooks.
In terms of support, I felt much more guided and supported compared to UCPH. At UCPH, there’s generally more responsibility placed on students, and you’re expected to be more self-reliant. At the host institution, the approach was more hands-on and supportive, which made the experience a bit easier. That said, I also took some units that are typically taken by students early in their studies at the host university, which might have influenced my experience and perception of the teaching style. Further there was a higher emphasis on assignments during the semester rather than just one big exam at the end, meaning the work-load was a bit more distributed.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PBH2003 - Culture, society and health

ATS1297 - Academic writing

PG5136 - Mindfulness for workplace wellbeing and productivity

APG5367 - Campaigns, advocacy and change

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I recommend all the units I took, but if I had to choose differently, I might have picked HSC2200 - Health across the Lifespan instead of Academic Writing. The units I took were all well-executed, interesting, and complemented my public health studies at UCPH very well.

• Academic Writing was good, but it didn’t have much engagement from other students, and most of the activities were led by the lecturer. The content was also quite introductory, which might not be as beneficial for someone who has already been studying for a while. While I did learn a lot about written English, I might have found Health across the Lifespan more enriching in terms of relevant theory for Public Health.

• PBH2003 - Culture, Society, and Health: This course provided valuable insights into Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders and gave a broader understanding of the Australian health and healthcare system.

• PG5136 - Mindfulness for Workplace Wellbeing and Productivity: This was a fantastic course with evidence-based techniques that I can use in my future job, studies, and personal life.

• APG5367 - Campaigns, Advocacy, and Change: I learned a lot about communication and advocacy, which I find applicable in various contexts when communication with the public and other institutions.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I encountered a few unexpected costs. I hadn’t initially budgeted for items such as towels, dishcloths, and cleaning cloths. Additionally, I needed to buy lunchbox wrapping, tupperwares, duvets, and pillows, as well as various kitchen essentials like pots and cups. These expenses added up more than I had anticipated. Furher as it felt like a big vacation you spend alot more than you would at home, especially since Australia is almost as expensive as Denmark.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I had a fairly clear idea of what things would cost in Australia beforehand. Most items, including food, are about 10% cheaper than in Denmark, but they’re still on the pricier side. Coffee, however, is significantly cheaper - about half the price compared to Denmark. For home essentials, you can find many affordable items at Kmart and IKEA.

On the other hand, most local experiences, for example boat trips to the Great Barrier Reef, turned out to be quite expensive. These activities can cost between 200-400 AUD per person, which was higher than I anticipated.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very satisfied with the range of non-academic opportunities available, such as clubs and sports. Although I didn’t make use of them personally, it was clear that there were plenty of options for those interested in such activities

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a wide variety of activities available, though most were centered at Clayton Campus, which wasn’t where I spent most of my time. While there were many opportunities to get involved, I didn’t actively participate in any of these campus-based events. Instead, I focused on the free events, festivals, and activities that took place frequently in and around Melbourne. These events were a great way to meet other exchange students, local students, and residents, and they contributed to a rich and enjoyable experience.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The free events, festivals, and activities that took place frequently in and around Melbourne CBD.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I recommend taking advantage of the many free events happening in and around Melbourne. You can find a good overview of these on the WhatsOn website, which lists festivals, markets, and more. Explore the beautiful hiking trails in the various mountain ranges and national parks around Melbourne, such as The Grampians, Werribee Gorge, Cathedral Ranges, and Wilsons Promontory National Park.

Be sure to visit the beaches south of Melbourne, especially Half Moon Bay Beach and Brighton Beach. A trip to Phillip Island is also worth it. For a broader Australian adventure, consider traveling around the country in a campervan, particularly along the East Coast to see the Great Barrier Reef, through the Outback, and to Tasmania during the summer.

Don’t miss driving the Great Ocean Road and visiting the many parks and lookouts in and around Melbourne, like Point Ormond. These activities offer a fantastic way to experience the natural beauty and diverse attractions Australia has to offer.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the local culture in Melbourne was relatively smooth. The city’s multicultural environment and the openness of Australians made it easy to adapt and feel welcome. While there were some challenges, like understanding local customs and navigating different social dynamics, these were manageable and part of the learning experience. Overall, the friendly and inclusive atmosphere helped me integrate and enjoy my time in Melbourne.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
To make the most of your social experience and connect with local students, start by engaging with those in student accommodations or visiting their places to meet new people. Take advantage of the many events and festivals happening in and around Melbourne - these gatherings are perfect for meeting both locals and fellow exchange students.

Joining campus activities, such as clubs and sports, can also be a great way to meet people with similar interests. Make sure to participate in orientation programs and university events, as these are designed to help you integrate and meet new friends.

Being open and proactive is key. Attend gatherings and activities organized by others, and don’t hesitate to take the initiative to join or organize hiking tours and other group trips that are frequently set up on Facebook. Lastly, maintaining a friendly and approachable attitude will help you connect with others and build meaningful relationships.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: One cultural difference that I found challenging was interacting with Indigenous people. Their historical background and strong sense of territory can make these interactions feel delicate, and there’s a concern about inadvertently offending or doing something wrong. Although there were relatively few Indigenous people on the streets, and most are not likely to cause harm, the presence of homeless people and those struggling with substance abuse in the evenings made me prefer not to walk around alone after dark. Despite this, I generally felt safe on the streets overall.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated the multiculturalism in Melbourne and the friendliness and openness of Australians and other residents. It was impressive how easy it was to strike up conversations with people everywhere, which made the experience feel welcoming and inclusive. Additionally, it was easy to build relationships and meet new people, contributing to a very positive and engaging experience.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Firstly, choose your campus wisely depending on whether you want to be close to Melbourne CBD or prefer more on-campus activities. Caulfield Campus is great for city access, while Clayton Campus offers more campus-based social options. Secondly, be prepared for potential housing challenges if you opt for private (off-campus) accommodation; secure your place early and have a backup plan in case your initial arrangements fall through. Lastly, actively engage in Melbourne’s local scene by attending events, joining clubs, and networking through social groups. Being proactive will significantly enhance your exchange experience.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you prefer to be close to Melbourne CBD, where most of the events and activities take place, Caulfield Campus is a great choice. It offers convenient access to the city and minimizes travel time. On the other hand, Clayton Campus provides more on-campus social activities and accommodation options, but it may involve longer travel time to the city. Many students at Clayton found themselves having to leave events early or split an Uber, as public transport options are limited in the evenings.

Consider what suits your lifestyle and interests best when choosing between the campuses. If you value proximity to the city and a more manageable travel time, Caulfield might be the better option. If you’re interested in a vibrant on-campus social scene and don’t mind the extra travel, Clayton could be ideal.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was everything about it - I would gladly do it all over again. The chance to immerse myself in a new culture, meet diverse people, study at a different university, and experience a different academic environment, along with exploring Melbourne and beyond as well as other parts of Australia, made the experience truly unforgettable.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge during my exchange was dealing with housing issues. Initially, the living situation with my first roommates didn’t work out, which led to the stress of finding new accommodation midway through my exchange. This added a layer of difficulty to my experience, as I had to balance the search for a new place with my studies and other activities. Despite this challenge, I managed to find another suitable place and continue enjoying my time abroad.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go for it and make the most of your time abroad—you will never regret it! Melbourne is the perfect place for an exchange in Australia.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
